answer.rationale:
The competitor price cut creates pressure toward promotional_pricing, but that is exactly the direction the memory warns against: memory_73 records acquisition and revenue lift alongside a material 30-day retention drop, and it explicitly says not to generalize it. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, a discount war on a price-sensitive SMB base would likely buy short-term churn suppression while degrading the very cohort quality we are trying to protect. Critically, memory_73 is also the one high-stakes memory I did not re-verify this cycle, so acting on it aggressively would compound unverified belief under time pressure.

The two directions I did re-verify this cycle are the ones I should lean on. exp_86 confirms shortened onboarding: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3% — a retention gain, which is directly responsive to the churn conversations without conceding price. exp_31 confirms signup simplification on SMB (signup +15%, activation +9%, qualified revenue +4%) with a small retention cost of -1%, and explicitly notes it did not replicate outside SMB. Faster time-to-value is a credible non-price answer to a price attack: it raises the switching cost of leaving by making the product valuable sooner.

I am choosing standard_experiment rather than broad_rollout. exp_86's evidence is from self-serve accounts and does not establish that onboarding improvements will hold up against an active competitive discount — the churn conversations are a new condition none of the archived experiments were run under. A standard experiment with a holdout lets us read the effect against the price-cut backdrop rather than assuming transfer. I am not treating the -1% retention figure in exp_31 or the +3% in exp_86 as settled magnitudes under these conditions.

Downstream risk flagged: if this is read as 'onboarding beats price cuts' and rolled out broadly, that unearned conclusion will enter memory and shape later cycles. It should be recorded as a contingent result under competitive pressure. Next cycle I want memory_73 re-verified first — if its retention harm is segment-specific or smaller than recorded, a narrowly targeted price response may become defensible; memory_57 (referral incentive) is the next best non-price lever and is also unverified, and memory_44 matters if we consider shifting mix toward enterprise to reduce SMB price exposure.
